Triggers.value: Water, flooding, or large bodies of water

Threat.value: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

vignette: Dr. Kwame Adeyemi had been teaching his graduate seminar when the call came. His younger brother, Tariq, had been trapped in their parents’ basement apartment after a burst pipe swelled into a sudden flood, drowning him in the rising dark. Kwame arrived to find the water seeping through the floorboards, the air thick with the sharp, metallic tang of wet concrete and old plumbing. He remembered standing at the threshold, watching the muddy tide creep toward the stairs, certain that the house would swallow everything if he did not move quickly enough. That week, the visual imprint of that creeping water stayed with him. When rain lashed against his car windows or a sprinkler system activated in the faculty lot, Kwame’s chest would tighten before his conscious mind registered the rain. His body was already bracing, his shoulders rising, his pulse drumming against his ribs, as if the basement were still filling. The smell of damp wool and wet earth from his brother’s last coat triggered a wave of horror that caught him mid-stride in the library stacks, forcing him to pause and grip a bookshelf until the wave passed. Over the following months, these reactions settled into a rhythm. Stress, whether from a mounting curriculum review or a stalled conversation, seemed to gather in his temples, making the world feel pressurized. He began to notice how his negative emotions surfaced without warning—a sharp pang of guilt when he remembered the phone call he had missed, a low simmer of anger at the insurance adjuster’s calm tone, a heavy shame that lingered in his throat after lectures when he thought he had seemed distracted. Even in his own quiet apartment, where the rugs were dry and the windows latched tight, Kwame could not relax. He would sit in his armchair, hands resting on his knees, aware that the room was safe, yet his breathing remained shallow and his gaze fixed on the hallway, waiting for something to shift. He had come to believe the water would rise again, not just outside, but inside his own steady days. His PCL-5 score of 54 mapped onto this lived reality, a clinical marker for the quiet exhaustion he carried. The avoidance formed gradually, a series of quiet departures: he declined the Friday reading circles, replaced them with solitary grading in his office, and found that the accumulated papers on his desk mirrored the way his own mind piled up, layer upon layer, waiting to be cleared. His academic environment became a landscape of familiar encounters. As a professor, his office overlooked the university’s central quad, where a decorative reflecting pool caught the afternoon light. During a departmental meeting, a colleague leaned too close, the scent of rain-dampened wool brushing past him. Kwame’s heart hammered against his sternum before he could identify the trigger. He excused himself, citing the need to review syllabi, and walked back to his desk. The stress of the semester’s grading deadlines pooled in his shoulders, compounding the visual weight of the water feature outside. He stopped attending the evening faculty receptions, finding the noise and the crowded rooms amplified his inability to settle. Instead, he marked his calendar with quiet precision, leaving his office by mid-afternoon to avoid the rush, his movements deliberate, his posture guarded. Now, at fifty-nine, Kwame remains single, living alone in a city apartment that smells faintly of leather and dried lavender. He does not know what the water in his apartment will do, or whether the dread will ever loosen its hold. What finally brought him to seek help was a Tuesday afternoon when he stood in his kitchen, staring at a half-full kettle, unable to pour the water into his cup. The sight of it, the quiet smell of wet ceramic, and the sudden spike of stress from an unanswered email left him standing in the doorway, his breath catching, his hands steady but his mind caught in the familiar loop. What frightened him most was the stillness itself—the way his body prepared for impact while his thoughts remained suspended. What he hoped for was simply to breathe without bracing, to walk through the day without waiting for the tide.
